essay.en: I arranged this shelf as a conversation between two old traditions that did not know of each other: the Chinese masters, from Laozi and Confucius to Zhuangzi and Xunzi, joined at the start of the twentieth century by Wang Guowei and Lu Xun; and the line that runs from Heraclitus and Plato through the Stoics, Montaigne and Bacon to Emerson and Thoreau. Most of these texts ask how to learn, how to read and how to live inside the limits of one life, which is why they belong in a library. Where an old English translation is the text, it is a historical one, such as George Long’s Marcus Aurelius, with my Chinese beside it; Legge’s versions of Laozi and Confucius stand next to the originals so that you can watch a text cross into another language. Begin with Zhuangzi’s cook, whose knife stays sharp for nineteen years and whose chapter ends with the fire passing on; then Montaigne’s two paragraphs to his reader; then Socrates, in the Phaedrus, warning that writing cannot answer back.
essay.zh: 我把这一架排成两支互不相识的古老思想之间的一场对话：一边是中国诸子，从老子、孔子到庄子、荀子，二十世纪初又来了王国维和鲁迅；一边是从赫拉克利特、柏拉图出发，经过斯多葛派、蒙田、培根，一直到爱默生和梭罗的那一脉。这些文字大多在问：怎样学，怎样读，怎样在一生的限度里活得好，所以它们属于图书馆。凡是以旧英译本为正文的，用的都是历史上的译本，比如乔治·朗译的马可·奥勒留，旁边的中文是我译的；理雅各译的老子和孔子，就摆在原文近旁，让你看一部书怎样走进另一种语言。从庄子笔下的庖丁读起，他的刀用了十九年还像新的一样，那一篇以“火传也”结尾；再读蒙田写给读者的那两段话；然后读《斐德若篇》里苏格拉底的提醒：文字不会回答你的问题。
